chapter_theme: The fourth part of Konganar's Vaalai Kummi turns from the goddess to the household: wife, children and parents are false and follow the dead only to the field and the burning-ground, so give while you can and finish your temple work before Death takes you off the mattress. A run of plain prohibitions follows (do not strike the poor, lie, steal, abuse devotees or covet chaste women), then caste is refuted by the one milk that becomes ghee, curd and buttermilk, and the part closes in riddles that only the one who has seen the mouthless horse can read.
structure_note: 1939 to 1942 are the gate, the seed and the false hut; 1943 to 1949 the falseness of kin and the duty of giving before death; 1950 to 1957 a list of do-nots in the manner of a conduct text, each stanza four prohibitions; 1958 and 1959 caste and offering; 1960 to 1963 riddles and the scholar who dies like anyone else.

1939.reading: If you see the inner gaze you can know; you can cross the four-and-six gates and open the locked door; this is not false but true, Vaalai girl.
1939.nuance: நாலாறு வாசல் is four-and-six, ten gates, or four-times-six, twenty-four; the body is usually given nine gates, and the tenth, closed, is the opening at the crown through which the yogi leaves, as tradition takes it. The locked door (பூட்டைக் கதவு) is then that tenth gate, and நாட்டம் the fixed inner gaze that opens it. A plain reading, that attention itself is the key, also stands.

1940.reading: You say a child came of man and woman joining; is it not that from man and woman joining there came one seed in which difference is gone?
1940.nuance: பேதம் அற்ற ஒரு வித்து, one seed without difference, carries the stanza: the plain sense is that every birth comes from the same undifferentiated seed, which prepares the caste argument of 1958; a coded sense takes the seed as bindu, the drop from which the body forms. The stanza does not choose.

1941.reading: What stands today is not false, nor is the house; that this is my life is not false; but it ends on that day as the writing says; so praise mother Vaalai.
1941.nuance: The stanza grants that the present and the house are real, against 1942 and 1943 which call them false; the two are reconciled by எழுத்தின்படி முடியும், the end written on the head. Konganar's point is not that life is illusion but that it is dated.

1942.reading: Do not wander in vain desire; this is not true, it is a false life and a false hut; if you find the unseen Vaalai you can see the vision and rule the sky.
1942.nuance: பொய்க்கூடு, the false hut, is the body, a usage shared with Punnakku Siddhar (2265, 2266). ஆகாயம் ஆளலாம் can be the siddhi of moving through space or the mastery of the inner space; the stanza allows both.

1943.reading: Is not becoming a wife false, and the children one bore false? The father who made much of you is false; is even the mother who gave the breast real?
1943.nuance: The question form (நிசமாமோ) leaves the mother last and hardest; the answer comes in 1944 and 1945, where she is matched with the wife and both are left at the boundary.

1944.reading: Mother and wife are alike, for both gave of their own body; but are the unripe and the ripe fruit the same? Look to your own intent, Vaalai girl.
1944.nuance: தன்யம் is unclear; read as தனம், the breast or one's substance, both women gave it. காயும் பழமும், green fruit and ripe, may distinguish the two gifts or the two women; the last line puts the difference in the looker's கருத்து, which recalls Pattinathar's resolve to see woman as mother.

1945.reading: The wife comes only as far as the common ground, the children one bore only as far as the burning-ground's edge; the dharma of service comes in between, joins you, and gives the highest state.
1945.nuance: மந்தை is the village common or cattle-ground at the edge of the settlement, the first boundary the funeral passes; the children go one boundary further. தொண்டாட்டுத் தர்மம் is dharma done as service, and it alone goes on.

1946.reading: If fortune, the enjoyment of offspring and royal enjoyment have come to you of themselves, do charity quickly and finish some temple work.
1946.nuance: மகள் போக்கியம் is odd; it may be a slip for மகா போக்கியம், great enjoyment, or mean the joy of daughters. The three goods are listed only to be spent: the stanza's verb is சீக்கிரம், quickly.

1947.reading: Those who have finished temple work are counted among those who, though they die, do not die: so Vaalai, who knows it, said in the grace-shining Veda.
1947.nuance: செத்தும் சாகாத பேர், those who die and do not die, is the Siddhar phrase for the undying; here it is promised to the temple-builder rather than the yogi, and the authority is Vaalai's own word called Veda.

1948.reading: While we lie on the mattress laughing with soft women, if warlike Death comes and seizes us, we too are only a dead corpse, Vaalai girl.

1949.reading: If a poor wretch has nothing and you have, you must give him food; you must not say 'tomorrow': so the four Vedas thunder.

1950.reading: Do not strike the poor and destitute, for that sin cannot be worn away; do not ruin those who said 'you are my refuge'; do not think of deceiving anyone.

1951.reading: Do not repeat what you saw and heard; do not give an answer about what your eye has not seen; do not tell your wife what has befallen you; do not belittle the children you bore.
1951.nuance: உற்றது in line 3 is what has happened to you, your troubles or secrets; கிளப்பம் in line 4 is read as இளப்பம், slight or disgrace. Both are guesses at a worn text; the first two lines, on hearsay and on speaking of the unseen, are clear.

1952.reading: Do not abuse Siva's devotees, Brahmins or the great ones of clear knowledge even in silence; do not do anything to pain their minds.
1952.nuance: மவுனமாகவும் வையாதே extends the prohibition from spoken abuse to the silent kind, the inner contempt; a Siddhar who elsewhere mocks Brahmins here lists them with devotees and gnanis among those not to be hurt.

1953.reading: Do not speak words that bring ruin in disputes; do not set your mind on chaste women; watch the breath you have practised, and praise Vaalai's feet.
1953.nuance: பழக்க வாசி, the vaasi of practice, is the one yogic term in the list of do-nots; tradition takes it as the regulated breath, and the stanza slips it between a rule of speech and a rule of praise as if it were a rule of conduct like the others.

1954.reading: Do not tell concerted lies; do not commit wicked robbery and theft; do not strike the dancing snake: this is wisdom, Vaalai girl.
1954.nuance: ஆடிய பாம்பை அடியாதே is plain advice (do not provoke a snake that has risen) and, in the Siddhar cipher, the coiled power that has begun to move, which is not to be forced. The stanza's own word for its content is அறிவு, practical wisdom, which favours the plain sense.

1955.reading: Even a man of deeds is not seen to speak boastfully, said Avvai; do not make mischief in the world: he who did fell shed like a ripe tamarind.
1955.nuance: The Avvai saying is not quoted exactly and the last line is loose; புளிப்பழம் போல் உதிர்ந்து, dropping like ripe tamarind, is the image of the braggart's fall. The first line could also be read as a question, 'has anyone seen a doer boast?'.

1956.reading: Do not make enemies of men of money; do not stand before a tiger in the deep forest; do not travel to foreign lands; do not take up the ways of an illusory courtesan.
1956.nuance: The four prohibitions are prudential, not spiritual; the one on foreign lands matches 1957, where wandering is folly because the goal is in one's own house.

1957.reading: Do not go to the neighbour's house while your own house stands; do not abuse mother and father; while the means is right inside your own house, you run about, Vaalai girl.
1957.nuance: ஊகம் (printed யூகம்), the thing to be reasoned out, is what lies in one's own house; read as cipher the house is the body and the thing within is the goddess or the breath, and the stanza becomes the usual Siddhar rebuke of pilgrimage. The plain reading, stay home and respect your parents, also stands, and the stanza pairs them deliberately.

1958.reading: You talk of caste differences; is there any difference in bodies that marks one as god? From the one milk that is spoken of came ghee, curd and buttermilk.
1958.nuance: The milk image makes castes products of one substance, as 1940 made every birth one seed. தெய்வம் தான் என்று ஒரு உடல் பேதம் உண்டோ asks whether any body is marked as divine, which is the ground on which caste rank is claimed.

1959.reading: The cat too has eaten the milk that was eaten; nothing higher is seen above it; cast off that desire for what is above and do your puja with longing in the heart.
1959.nuance: The first two lines are obscure. One reading: the milk offered to the god is drunk by the cat, and no higher taker is seen, so the outward offering is futile and worship belongs within. The stanza's advice in lines 3 and 4 is clear whatever the image.

1960.reading: I said the hen has six legs; I said the hunchback of the east has three legs; I said the hunchback has two letters; I said the whole pot has no mouth.
1960.nuance: A chain of riddles whose keys are withheld, in the manner of the Siddhar cipher; 1961 and 1962 show that the hearer is being tested, and 1962 names the mouthless horse, the breath, as the key to the beasts. The pot with no mouth is in other Siddhar verses the closed body or the sealed crown; the hen and the hunchback are not explained here, and no tradition is cited for them.

1961.reading: I said the goat has two legs; our pot stands on a pot, with a womb above; I said the cow has no legs: tell me the kinds in the tale, Vaalai girl.
1961.nuance: Line 2 is corrupt (பானைக்குப் பானைக்கு) and மேல்சூல் is unclear, perhaps the belly or womb set above the pot. The stanza's demand, கதை வகையைச் சொல்லடி, makes the riddles a test of the hearer's initiation rather than a teaching.

1962.reading: The one who robbed the temple and the cow, the one who has learned the noise of shouting, and the one who has seen the mouthless horse: does he know the kinds of cattle, Vaalai girl?
1962.nuance: வாயில்லாக் குதிரை, the horse without a mouth, is the breath in the Siddhar cipher (the horse that is reined but not fed), as tradition takes it; the stanza asks whether even such a one can read the riddle-beasts of 1960 and 1961. The syntax is loose and the three men may be one or three.

1963.reading: If people who have studied all these sastras die, the world will laugh; even in dying he must mingle, he must join the gods.
1963.nuance: The scholar is mocked not for learning but for dying like anyone else; the Siddhar standard is that true knowledge shows in the manner of death, joining rather than ending. The 'he' of line 3 is the knower, in contrast to the learned who die.

links.note: Pattinathar says wife, children and wealth reach only as far as one's own mouth and kin as far as the cremation ground, and that a sesame seed of austerity rules the road; Konganar says the wife comes to the common ground and the children to the burning-ground's edge, and the dharma of service joins one in between. Both measure kin by the boundary they stop at and name a single companion that goes on.

Pattinathar asks who would trust this birth while the hoard lies there and the wife is at the door, having seen the death-rattle; Konganar says Death may seize us as we laugh with soft women on the mattress and we are at once a corpse. Both set the deathbed in the midst of enjoyment, not after it.

The Naladiyar tells the wealthy to give, since the span cannot be exceeded and tomorrow the funeral drum may sound; Konganar says the one who has must feed the one who has not and must not say 'tomorrow', and gives the four Vedas as authority. Both make the urgency of giving rest on the nearness of death.

The Kural says do virtue without saying 'later', for it is the companion that does not perish; Konganar says that if fortune has come, do charity quickly and finish temple work, and 1947 adds that those who finish it do not die. Both make haste the whole of the counsel; the Kural's reward is a companion at death, Konganar's a kind of deathlessness.

Sivavakkiyar asks what is a Paraiyar woman and what a Brahmin woman, whether a number is marked on flesh, skin or bone; Konganar asks whether any body carries a difference marking it as god, and says ghee, curd and buttermilk come from one milk. Both deny caste by appeal to the body's sameness; Sivavakkiyar's test is pleasure, Konganar's the common source.

The Naladiyar says cows differ in colour but their milk does not, so virtue is one though its ways are many; Konganar says the one milk became ghee, curd and buttermilk, so caste differences are products of one substance. The image runs the opposite way: in the Naladiyar many sources give one thing, in Konganar one source gives many.

Pattinathar says that while the Lord of Arur is right here people wander from town to town for festivals, looking for fire while the lamp burns; Konganar says that while the means is inside your own house you run about to the neighbour's. Both make wandering the failure to look where one already is; the kummi keeps the plain sense of house and neighbour alongside the coded one.

Sivavakkiyar asks the sastra-reciting Bhattar whether the Veda will help when the sweat and gasping come; Konganar says the world laughs when those who studied all the sastras die like anyone, and that the knower must join the gods even in dying. Both test learning at the moment of death and find it wanting.

source_issues: 1946 line 1 மகள் போக்கியம் is probably a slip for மகா போக்கியம்.
1951 line 4 கிளப்பம் is not a word; read as இளப்பம்.
1957 line 3 யூகம் is a spelling of ஊகம்.
1960 line 2 கூனிக் மூன்றுகால் has broken sandhi (for கூனிக்கு மூன்று கால்); the riddle text of 1960 to 1962 is worn throughout.
1961 line 2 பானைக்குப் பானைக்குநிற்கு மேல்சூல் is corrupt, with a doubled word and no clear construction.
1955 line 4 புளிப் பழம்போ லுதிர்த்து விழுந்தானே is loosely attached to the stanza and may be a half-remembered proverb.
